newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka relies on coal in $2 bln power plan.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka relies on coal in $2 bln power plan.

text.p: Sri Lanka plans to invest up to $2 billion to build new power plants in the next decade and will rely heavily on coal for future energy needs, a state power utility official said on Thursday.
The Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) will build only one new hydroelectric plant under its plan to add almost 700 megawatts of power to the national grid by 2002, he said.
The rest of the energy will come from diesel, gas turbine, combined cycle and coal power plants, with another 600 MW from coal over the next four years, he said.

The Indian Ocean island suffered severe power shortages this year and its 10-year plan will virtually double the present power generating capacity of about 1,250 MW -- 84 percent from hydroelectric plants and the balance from thermal plants.
"In the next 10 years we'll need something like $2 billion in investment to build new power plants," said the official who declined to be identified.
Most of the new plants would be on build-operate-own or build-operate-transfer terms, he added.

The CEB planned two or more diesel plants supplying 90 MW by 1998, several combined cycle plants (gas and steam turbines) providing 300 MW by 1999 and two 150 MW coal plants by 2002, the official said.
"It will be all coal (after 2002) unless we go for nuclear power which is unlikely as the country is too small," he said.
The CEB's plan to add another 600 MW of coal power after 2002 would raise total coal power generation by 2006 to 900 MW, he said.

Sri Lanka faced a severe power crisis earlier this year, with daily power cuts of upto eight hours, after monsoon rains failed, forcing the government to put clocks forward by an hour in May to make maximum use of daylight.
The government announced on Thursday it had decided to put back the clock by half an hour from midnight Friday because the power crisis was over and late sunrise in the winter months.
The power crunch was attributed to delays in building new power plants to meet rising demand.
The CEB will go ahead with plans to build a 70 MW hydroelectric plant in the central hills but has shelved a 150 MW hydropower plant in the same region for environmental reasons, the official said.

Italy's Fiat Avio is building a 115 MW gas turbine plant at the CEB's Kelanitissa power station to come on stream by mid-1997 while Germany's B&W Diesel AG is building a 40 MW diesel plant to be commissioned around the same time, he added.
KHD Great Britain Ltd, a unit of Germany's Klockner-Humboldt-Deutz AG, is building $62 million 51 MW diesel power plant, also expected to be commissioned by mid-1997.
